# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Badges

Source: https://docs.rs/about/badges

Docs.rs no longer has its own badges. Consider using [shields.io](https://shields.io) instead.

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# base64 0.22.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/base64/^0.22.1

Made with CLion. Thanks to JetBrains for supporting open source!

It's base64. What more could anyone want?

This library's goals are to be *correct* and *fast*. It's thoroughly tested and widely used. It exposes functionality at
multiple levels of abstraction so you can choose the level of convenience vs performance that you want,
e.g. `decode_engine_slice` decodes into an existing `&mut [u8]` and is pretty fast (2.6GiB/s for a 3 KiB input),
whereas `decode_engine` allocates a new `Vec<u8>` and returns it, which might be more convenient in some cases, but is
slower (although still fast enough for almost any purpose) at 2.1 GiB/s.

See the [docs](https://docs.rs/base64) for all the details.

## FAQ

### I need to decode base64 with whitespace/null bytes/other random things interspersed in it. What should I do?

Remove non-base64 characters from your input before decoding.

If you have a `Vec` of base64, [retain](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/vec/struct.Vec.html#method.retain) can be used to
strip out whatever you need removed.

If you have a `Read` (e.g. reading a file or network socket), there are various approaches.

- Use [iter_read](https://crates.io/crates/iter-read)together with`Read`'s`bytes()`to filter out unwanted bytes.
- Implement `Read`with a`read()`impl that delegates to your actual`Read`, and then drops any bytes you don't want.

### I need to line-wrap base64, e.g. for MIME/PEM.

[line-wrap](https://crates.io/crates/line-wrap) does just that.

### I want canonical base64 encoding/decoding.

First, don't do this. You should no more expect Base64 to be canonical than you should expect compression algorithms to
produce canonical output across all usage in the wild (hint: they don't).
However, [people are drawn to their own destruction like moths to a flame](https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/361), so here we
are.

There are two opportunities for non-canonical encoding (and thus, detection of the same during decoding): the final bits
of the last encoded token in two or three token suffixes, and the `=` token used to inflate the suffix to a full four
tokens.

The trailing bits issue is unavoidable: with 6 bits available in each encoded token, 1 input byte takes 2 tokens, with the second one having some bits unused. Same for two input bytes: 16 bits, but 3 tokens have 18 bits. Unless we decide to stop shipping whole bytes around, we're stuck with those extra bits that a sneaky or buggy encoder might set to 1 instead of 0.

The `=` pad bytes, on the other hand, are entirely a self-own by the Base64 standard. They do not affect decoding other
than to provide an opportunity to say "that padding is incorrect". Exabytes of storage and transfer have no doubt been
wasted on pointless `=` bytes. Somehow we all seem to be quite comfortable with, say, hex-encoded data just stopping
when it's done rather than requiring a confirmation that the author of the encoder could count to four. Anyway, there
are two ways to make pad bytes predictable: require canonical padding to the next multiple of four bytes as per the RFC,
or, if you control all producers and consumers, save a few bytes by requiring no padding (especially applicable to the
url-safe alphabet).

All `Engine` implementations must at a minimum support treating non-canonical padding of both types as an error, and
optionally may allow other behaviors.

## Rust version compatibility

The minimum supported Rust version is 1.48.0.

# Contributing

Contributions are very welcome. However, because this library is used widely, and in security-sensitive contexts, all PRs will be carefully scrutinized. Beyond that, this sort of low level library simply needs to be 100% correct. Nobody wants to chase bugs in encoding of any sort.

All this means that it takes me a fair amount of time to review each PR, so it might take quite a while to carve out the free time to give each PR the attention it deserves. I will get to everyone eventually!

## Developing

Benchmarks are in `benches/`.

```
```
## no_std

This crate supports no_std. By default the crate targets std via the `std` feature. You can deactivate
the `default-features` to target `core` instead. In that case you lose out on all the functionality revolving
around `std::io`, `std::error::Error`, and heap allocations. There is an additional `alloc` feature that you can activate
to bring back the support for heap allocations.

## Profiling

On Linux, you can use [perf](https://perf.wiki.kernel.org/index.php/Main_Page) for profiling. Then compile the
benchmarks with `cargo bench --no-run`.

Run the benchmark binary with `perf` (shown here filtering to one particular benchmark, which will make the results
easier to read). `perf` is only available to the root user on most systems as it fiddles with event counters in your
CPU, so use `sudo`. We need to run the actual benchmark binary, hence the path into `target`. You can see the actual
full path with `cargo bench -v`; it will print out the commands it runs. If you use the exact path
that `bench` outputs, make sure you get the one that's for the benchmarks, not the tests. You may also want
to `cargo clean` so you have only one `benchmarks-` binary (they tend to accumulate).

You'll see a bunch of interleaved rust source and assembly like this. The section with `lib.rs:327` is telling us that
4.02% of samples saw the `movzbl` aka bit shift as the active instruction. However, this percentage is not as exact as
it seems due to a phenomenon called *skid*. Basically, a consequence of how fancy modern CPUs are is that this sort of
instruction profiling is inherently inaccurate, especially in branch-heavy code.

# bs58 0.5.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/bs58/^0.5.1

Another Rust [Base58](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Base58) codec implementation.

Compared to [ base58](https://github.com/debris/base58) this is significantly faster at decoding (about
2.4x as fast when decoding 32 bytes), almost the same speed for encoding
(about 3% slower when encoding 32 bytes), doesn't have the 128 byte
limitation and supports a configurable alphabet.

Compared to [ rust-base58](https://github.com/nham/rust-base58) this is massively faster (over ten times as
fast when decoding 32 bytes, almost 40 times as fast when encoding 32
bytes), has no external dependencies and supports a configurable alphabet.

# Rust Version Policy

This crate only supports the current stable version of Rust, patch releases may use new features at any time.

or [#beginners](https://discord.com/channels/442252698964721669/448238009733742612) channels of the official Rust Project Discord (invite:

repo but they tend not to get as many eyes as any of the above and may get

- [JSON API documentation](https://docs.rs/serde_json)
- [Serde API documentation](https://docs.rs/serde)
- [Detailed documentation about Serde](https://serde.rs/)
- [Setting up](https://serde.rs/derive.html)- `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]`
- [Release notes](https://github.com/serde-rs/json/releases)

JSON is a ubiquitous open-standard format that uses human-readable text to transmit data objects consisting of key-value pairs.

```
```
There are three common ways that you might find yourself needing to work with JSON data in Rust.

- **As text data.**An unprocessed string of JSON data that you receive on an HTTP endpoint, read from a file, or prepare to send to a remote server.
- **As an untyped or loosely typed representation.**Maybe you want to check that some JSON data is valid before passing it on, but without knowing the structure of what it contains. Or you want to do very basic manipulations like insert a key in a particular spot.
- **As a strongly typed Rust data structure.**When you expect all or most of your data to conform to a particular structure and want to get real work done without JSON's loosey-goosey nature tripping you up.

Serde JSON provides efficient, flexible, safe ways of converting data between each of these representations.

## Operating on untyped JSON values

Any valid JSON data can be manipulated in the following recursive enum
representation. This data structure is [ serde_json::Value](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/value/enum.Value.html).

```
```
A string of JSON data can be parsed into a `serde_json::Value` by the
[ serde_json::from_str](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/de/fn.from_str.html) function. There is also

[for parsing from a byte slice](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/de/fn.from_slice.html)

`from_slice``&[u8]` and
[for parsing from any](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/de/fn.from_reader.html)

`from_reader``io::Read` like a File or a
TCP stream.```
use ;
```
The result of square bracket indexing like `v["name"]` is a borrow of the data
at that index, so the type is `&Value`. A JSON map can be indexed with string
keys, while a JSON array can be indexed with integer keys. If the type of the
data is not right for the type with which it is being indexed, or if a map does
not contain the key being indexed, or if the index into a vector is out of
bounds, the returned element is `Value::Null`.

When a `Value` is printed, it is printed as a JSON string. So in the code above,
the output looks like `Please call "John Doe" at the number "+44 1234567"`. The
quotation marks appear because `v["name"]` is a `&Value` containing a JSON
string and its JSON representation is `"John Doe"`. Printing as a plain string
without quotation marks involves converting from a JSON string to a Rust string
with [ as_str()](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/enum.Value.html#method.as_str) or avoiding the use of

`Value` as described in the following
section.The `Value` representation is sufficient for very basic tasks but can be tedious
to work with for anything more significant. Error handling is verbose to
implement correctly, for example imagine trying to detect the presence of
unrecognized fields in the input data. The compiler is powerless to help you
when you make a mistake, for example imagine typoing `v["name"]` as `v["nmae"]`
in one of the dozens of places it is used in your code.

## Parsing JSON as strongly typed data structures

Serde provides a powerful way of mapping JSON data into Rust data structures largely automatically.

```
use ;
use Result;
```
This is the same `serde_json::from_str` function as before, but this time we
assign the return value to a variable of type `Person` so Serde will
automatically interpret the input data as a `Person` and produce informative
error messages if the layout does not conform to what a `Person` is expected to
look like.

Any type that implements Serde's `Deserialize` trait can be deserialized this
way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>` and
`HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Deserialize)]`.

Once we have `p` of type `Person`, our IDE and the Rust compiler can help us use
it correctly like they do for any other Rust code. The IDE can autocomplete
field names to prevent typos, which was impossible in the `serde_json::Value`
representation. And the Rust compiler can check that when we write
`p.phones[0]`, then `p.phones` is guaranteed to be a `Vec<String>` so indexing
into it makes sense and produces a `String`.

The necessary setup for using Serde's derive macros is explained on the * Using
derive* page of the Serde site.

## Constructing JSON values

Serde JSON provides a [ json! macro](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/macro.json.html) to build

`serde_json::Value`
objects with very natural JSON syntax.```
use json;
```
The `Value::to_string()` function converts a `serde_json::Value` into a `String`
of JSON text.

One neat thing about the `json!` macro is that variables and expressions can be
interpolated directly into the JSON value as you are building it. Serde will
check at compile time that the value you are interpolating is able to be
represented as JSON.

```
let full_name = "John Doe";
let age_last_year = 42;
// The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
let john = json!;
```
This is amazingly convenient, but we have the problem we had before with
`Value`: the IDE and Rust compiler cannot help us if we get it wrong. Serde JSON
provides a better way of serializing strongly-typed data structures into JSON
text.

## Creating JSON by serializing data structures

A data structure can be converted to a JSON string by
[ serde_json::to_string](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/ser/fn.to_string.html). There is also

[which serializes to a](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/ser/fn.to_vec.html)

`serde_json::to_vec``Vec<u8>` and
[which serializes to any](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/ser/fn.to_writer.html)

`serde_json::to_writer``io::Write`
such as a File or a TCP stream.```
use ;
use Result;
```
Any type that implements Serde's `Serialize` trait can be serialized this way.
This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>` and `HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with `#[derive(Serialize)]`.

## Performance

It is fast. You should expect in the ballpark of 500 to 1000 megabytes per
second deserialization and 600 to 900 megabytes per second serialization,
depending on the characteristics of your data. This is competitive with the
fastest C and C++ JSON libraries or even 30% faster for many use cases.
Benchmarks live in the [serde-rs/json-benchmark](https://github.com/serde-rs/json-benchmark) repo.

## Getting help

Serde is one of the most widely used Rust libraries, so any place that
Rustaceans congregate will be able to help you out. For chat, consider trying
the [#rust-questions](https://discord.com/channels/273534239310479360/274215136414400513) or [#rust-beginners](https://discord.com/channels/273534239310479360/273541522815713281) channels of the unofficial community
Discord (invite: [https://discord.gg/rust-lang-community](https://discord.gg/rust-lang-community)), the [#rust-usage](https://discord.com/channels/442252698964721669/443150878111694848) or
[#beginners](https://discord.com/channels/442252698964721669/448238009733742612) channels of the official Rust Project Discord (invite:
[https://discord.gg/rust-lang](https://discord.gg/rust-lang)), or the [#general](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/122651-general) stream in Zulip. For
asynchronous, consider the [[rust] tag on StackOverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/rust), the
[/r/rust](https://www.reddit.com/r/rust) subreddit which has a pinned weekly easy questions post, or the Rust
[Discourse forum](https://users.rust-lang.org). It's acceptable to file a support issue in this
repo, but they tend not to get as many eyes as any of the above and may get
closed without a response after some time.

## No-std support

As long as there is a memory allocator, it is possible to use serde_json without the rest of the Rust standard library. Disable the default "std" feature and enable the "alloc" feature:

```
[]
 = {  = "1.0",  = false,  = ["alloc"] }
```
For JSON support in Serde without a memory allocator, please see the
[ serde-json-core](https://github.com/rust-embedded-community/serde-json-core) crate.

# zstd 0.13.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/zstd/^0.13.3

# zstd

This library is a rust binding for the [zstd compression library](https://github.com/facebook/zstd).

## 1 - Add to `cargo.toml`

```
```
```
# Cargo.toml
[]
 = "0.13"
```
## 2 - Usage

This library provides `Read` and `Write` wrappers to handle (de)compression,
along with convenience functions to made common tasks easier.

For instance, `stream::copy_encode` and `stream::copy_decode` are easy-to-use
wrappers around `std::io::copy`. Check the [stream](https://docs.rs/examples/stream.rs) example:

```
use io;
// This function use the convenient `copy_encode` method
// This function does the same thing, directly using an `Encoder`:
```
# Asynchronous support

The [ async-compression](https://github.com/Nemo157/async-compression/) crate
provides an async-ready integration of various compression algorithms,
including

`zstd-rs`.# Compile it yourself

`zstd` is included as a submodule. To get everything during your clone, use:

```
git clone https://github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs --recursive
```
Or, if you cloned it without the `--recursive` flag,
call this from inside the repository:

```
git submodule update --init
```
Then, running `cargo build` should take care
of building the C library and linking to it.

# Build-time bindgen

This library includes a pre-generated `bindings.rs` file.
You can also generate new bindings at build-time, using the `bindgen` feature:

```
cargo build --features bindgen
```

# Disclaimer

This implementation is largely inspired by bozaro's [lz4-rs](https://github.com/bozaro/lz4-rs).

facett-map3d-flight-0.1.10

facett — AAA planetary FLIGHT-SIM engine layer over facett-map3d: f64 floating origin (camera-relative rebase, kills far-from-origin jitter), precomputed atmospheric scattering (Bruneton/Hillaire-style transmittance LUT + sky-view + aerial perspective), and a 6DOF camera rig (free-fly / cinematic-orbit / flight-stick). GPU-required, full-screen, opt-in — the lightweight embeddable map stays in facett-map3d. Reuses (does not fork) facett-map3d's Mesh3 + wgpu pipeline.

# pivx_rpc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pivx-rpc/0.4.0/pivx_rpc/

## Expand description

PIVX SDK: typed JSON-RPC client for pivxd with first-class support for shielded (SHIELD/Sapling) balances and transactions.

```
use pivx_rpc::{Auth, PivxClient, ShieldRecipient, ShieldWatcher, WatchOptions};
let client = PivxClient::new(
    "http://127.0.0.1:51473",
    Auth::UserPass { user: "rpcuser".into(), pass: "rpcpass".into() },
)?;
// Watch a shielded address via its viewing key (no spend key needed).
let imported = client.import_sapling_viewing_key("p-view-key...", None, None).await?;
let mut watcher = ShieldWatcher::new(&client, WatchOptions {
    addresses: vec![imported.address],
    ..Default::default()
});
let events = watcher.poll().await?; // first poll primes silently
// Send shielded funds (node wallet holds the keys and builds the proof).
let txid = client
    .shield_send_many(
        pivx_rpc::FromAddress::AnyShield,
        &[ShieldRecipient::new("ps1...", 1.5).with_memo("hello")],
    )
    .await?;
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Block](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockHeader.html)- Header
- Verbose block header (`getblockheader`, verbose=true). For the raw serialized header use`get_block`with verbosity 0.
- [Block](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockIndexStats.html)- Index - Stats
- `getblockindexstats`. Note the space-keyed field names and that- `ttlfee`/- `feeperkb`are money- **strings**(- `FormatMoney`), not numbers.
- [Blockchain](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockchainInfo.html)- Info
- [Budget](https://docs.rs/struct.BudgetProjection.html)- Projection
- Element of `getbudgetprojection`: a`BudgetProposal``TotalBudgetAllotted`.
- [Budget](https://docs.rs/struct.BudgetProposal.html)- Proposal
- Element of `getbudgetinfo`. Field names are the node’s exact PascalCase keys.
- [Chain](https://docs.rs/struct.ChainTip.html)- Tip
- One entry of `getchaintips`.
- [Decoded](https://docs.rs/struct.DecodedTransaction.html)- Transaction
- Decoded transaction (`decoderawtransaction`, verbose`getrawtransaction`).
- [Estimate](https://docs.rs/struct.EstimateSmartFee.html)- Smart - Fee
- `estimatesmartfee`.
- [Imported](https://docs.rs/struct.ImportedSaplingKey.html)- Sapling - Key
- Result of `importsaplingkey`/`importsaplingviewingkey`.
- [List](https://docs.rs/struct.ListSinceBlock.html)- Since - Block
- Result of `list_since_block`. PIVX omits the`removed`array.
- [List](https://docs.rs/struct.ListTransaction.html)- Transaction
- Element of `list_transactions`/`list_since_block`(long form: the listtransactions fields plus the embedded wallet-tx fields).
- [Local](https://docs.rs/struct.LocalAddress.html)- Address
- [Mempool](https://docs.rs/struct.MempoolEntry.html)- Entry
- Verbose `getrawmempool`entry (value of the txid-keyed map).
- [Mempool](https://docs.rs/struct.MempoolInfo.html)- Info
- `getmempoolinfo`.
- [Mining](https://docs.rs/struct.MiningInfo.html)- Info
- `getmininginfo`. In normal mode the node emits both- `errors`and- `warnings`(with- `-deprecatedrpc=getmininginfo`only- `errors`), so- `warnings`is optional.
- [Network](https://docs.rs/struct.NetworkEntry.html)- Entry
- [Network](https://docs.rs/struct.NetworkInfo.html)- Info
- `getnetworkinfo`.
- [Peer](https://docs.rs/struct.PeerInfo.html)- Info
- Element of `getpeerinfo`.
- [Pivx](https://docs.rs/struct.PivxClient.html)- Client
- Async JSON-RPC client for a pivxd node.
- [PrevTx](https://docs.rs/struct.PrevTx.html)
- Previous-output spec for `sign_raw_transaction`.
- [Received](https://docs.rs/struct.ReceivedShieldNote.html)- Shield - Note
- Received note, as returned by `listreceivedbyshieldaddress`.
- [Script](https://docs.rs/struct.ScriptPubKey.html)- PubKey
- Script of a transaction output (`gettxout`, decoded-tx vout).
- [Script](https://docs.rs/struct.ScriptSig.html)- Sig
- [Shield](https://docs.rs/struct.ShieldNote.html)- Note
- Unspent shielded note, as returned by `listshieldunspent`.
- [Shield](https://docs.rs/struct.ShieldPoolValue.html)- Pool - Value
- [Shield](https://docs.rs/struct.ShieldRecipient.html)- Recipient
- Recipient entry for `shieldsendmany`/`rawshieldsendmany`.
- [Shield](https://docs.rs/struct.ShieldTxOutput.html)- TxOutput
- [Shield](https://docs.rs/struct.ShieldTxSpend.html)- TxSpend
- [Shield](https://docs.rs/struct.ShieldTxView.html)- TxView
- Decrypted view of a shielded transaction (`viewshieldtransaction`).
- [Shield](https://docs.rs/struct.ShieldWatcher.html)- Watcher
- Polls the node and reports `ShieldEvent`
- [Sign](https://docs.rs/struct.SignError.html)- Error
- [Sign](https://docs.rs/struct.SignRawTransactionResult.html)- RawTransaction - Result
- Result of `sign_raw_transaction`.
- [Staking](https://docs.rs/struct.StakingAddress.html)- Address
- Element of `liststakingaddresses`.
- [Staking](https://docs.rs/struct.StakingStatus.html)- Status
- `getstakingstatus`(PIVX wallet).- `lastattempt_*`are present only after a staking attempt.
- [Supply](https://docs.rs/struct.SupplyInfo.html)- Info
- `getsupplyinfo`(PIVX-specific).
- [Transaction](https://docs.rs/struct.Transaction.html)
- Wallet’s record of a transaction (`gettransaction`).
- [Transaction](https://docs.rs/struct.TransactionDetail.html)- Detail
- Short detail element embedded in `gettransaction`.
- [TxInput](https://docs.rs/struct.TxInput.html)
- Input spec for `create_raw_transaction`.
- [TxOut](https://docs.rs/struct.TxOut.html)
- Unspent output details (`gettxout`); the call returns`None`when spent or not found.
- [Unspent](https://docs.rs/struct.Unspent.html)
- [Validate](https://docs.rs/struct.ValidateAddress.html)- Address
- Result of `validate_address`. Only`isvalid`is guaranteed; the rest depend on validity and address type (transparent vs shield).
- [Vin](https://docs.rs/struct.Vin.html)
- Input of a decoded transaction. Coinbase inputs carry `coinbase`; every other input carries`txid`/`vout`/`script_sig`.
- [Vout](https://docs.rs/struct.Vout.html)
- Output of a decoded transaction.
- [Wallet](https://docs.rs/struct.WalletInfo.html)- Info
- [Watch](https://docs.rs/struct.WatchOptions.html)- Options
- Options for `ShieldWatcher`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Auth](https://docs.rs/enum.Auth.html)
- Authentication for the node’s RPC interface.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- [From](https://docs.rs/enum.FromAddress.html)- Address
- Source for `shieldsendmany`: an address or a selector.
- [Shield](https://docs.rs/enum.ShieldEvent.html)- Event
- Change observed in the wallet’s shielded note set.

# sim_lib_pitch_namer - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-pitch-namer/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_pitch_namer/

## Expand description

Multi-school cluster naming for the SIM music libraries.

This crate is the aggregator over the pitch-naming schools. It defines the
shared [ ClusterNamer](https://docs.rs/trait.ClusterNamer.html) trait and the

[taxonomy, then drives every built-in school – Forte set-class names, functional roman numerals, plain set-theory prime forms, neo-Riemannian labels, and jazz chord symbols – through one](https://docs.rs/enum.NamingSchool.html)

`NamingSchool`[. The registry can label a pitch-class set in every school at once and translate a label from one school to another. The schools themselves live in the](https://docs.rs/struct.NamerRegistry.html)

`NamerRegistry``sim-lib-pitch-namer-*` sibling crates; this
crate composes them and exposes them as a SIM runtime library through
[/](https://docs.rs/struct.PitchNamerLib.html)

`PitchNamerLib`[.](https://docs.rs/fn.install_pitch_namer_lib.html)

`install_pitch_namer_lib`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Cluster](https://docs.rs/struct.ClusterLabel.html)- Label
- A label produced by one naming school for one pitch-class set.
- [Cluster](https://docs.rs/struct.ClusterMeta.html)- Meta
- Metadata attached to a produced `ClusterLabel`
- [Label](https://docs.rs/struct.LabelContext.html)- Context
- The context a namer may use: an optional chord root and an optional key.
- [Namer](https://docs.rs/struct.NamerRegistry.html)- Registry
- A registry of `ClusterNamer`
- [Pitch](https://docs.rs/struct.PitchNamerLib.html)- Namer - Lib
- Host-registered lib exporting the built-in cluster-namer cards and registry,
built on the shared `SurfacePackLib`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Naming](https://docs.rs/enum.NamingSchool.html)- School
- A school of chord and pitch-set naming.
- [Pitch](https://docs.rs/enum.PitchNamerError.html)- Namer - Error
- Error returned by naming-registry operations.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Cluster](https://docs.rs/trait.ClusterNamer.html)- Namer
- A namer that labels a pitch-class set within one `NamingSchool`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [install_](https://docs.rs/fn.install_pitch_namer_lib.html)- pitch_ - namer_ - lib
- Installs the `PitchNamerLib``cx`, registering each namer’s export record; installing more than once is a no-op.

---

# facett - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett/0.1.10/facett/

## Expand description

**facett** — umbrella crate. One dependency that re-exports every component,
so a consumer writes `facett::graph::GraphView` / `facett::map::MapView` etc.
instead of pulling each `facett-*` crate. The `Facet` model + the headless
test `harness` are at the root.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [facett_core](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/index.html)as core;
- `pub use`- [facett_arrow](https://docs.rs/facett-arrow/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_arrow/index.html)as arrow;
- `pub use`- [facett_card](https://docs.rs/facett-card/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_card/index.html)as card;
- `pub use`- [facett_console](https://docs.rs/facett-console/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_console/index.html)as console;
- `pub use`- [facett_filedialog](https://docs.rs/facett-filedialog/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_filedialog/index.html)as filedialog;
- `pub use`- [facett_video](https://docs.rs/facett-video/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_video/index.html)as video;
- `pub use`- [facett_docview](https://docs.rs/facett-docview/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_docview/index.html)as docview;
- `pub use`- [facett_form](https://docs.rs/facett-form/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_form/index.html)as form;
- `pub use`- [facett_graph](https://docs.rs/facett-graph/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_graph/index.html)as graph;
- `pub use`- [facett_graph3d](https://docs.rs/facett-graph3d/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_graph3d/index.html)as graph3d;
- `pub use`- [facett_map](https://docs.rs/facett-map/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_map/index.html)as map;

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [clip](https://docs.rs/clip/index.html)
- **Cross-facet typed copy/paste**(§16) — the trait + payload machinery so copy/paste carries- **full typed data**between facett components, not just text. A process-wide transfer registry holds the last typed- `ClipPayload`
- [effects](https://docs.rs/effects/index.html)
- **effects**— motion + bloom for the facett look. Pure egui,- **glow backend only**: everything here paints with layered alpha shapes on an- `egui::Painter`
- [harness](https://docs.rs/harness/index.html)
- Headless test harness — **fire up a**: its`Facet`, inject data, render it offscreen, and capture what it drew`state_json`+ a vertex count (a “it drew something” proxy) + a stderr activity trail. No display, no GPU. This is the basis of facett’s auto test matrix, and mirrors nornir viz’s`NORNIR_VIZ_STATE`introspection — every component is observable from outside.
- [look](https://docs.rs/look/index.html)
- **facett look & feel**(the work-order architecture, §3) — one- `Theme`- **Windows**,- **macOS**,- **Device**(effects-off, rugged/military). The- `Theme`- *single source of truth*:- `Theme::apply`- `egui::Style`(visuals + spacing + scroll) plus the text scale in one call, and also publishes the derived legacy- `crate::Theme`
- [nav](https://docs.rs/nav/index.html)
- **Shared spatial navigation + focus**(§13 FOC-2, §14 NAV-1) — the- *one*pan/zoom model (- `Navigable`) reused by map/graph/plot/canvas, and the- *one*spatial focus rule (- `nearest_in_direction`) reused by pane and form navigation (COH-3). Pan/zoom is expressed as an- `egui::emath::TSTransform`(scale + offset), so a host can also use it to transform an overlaid guest layer (§5 CMP-4).
- [scroll_](https://docs.rs/scroll_engine/index.html)- engine
- **CygnusEd smooth-scroll engine**(§11) — pixel-by-pixel, sub-pixel soft scrolling with momentum/acceleration, à la the Amiga editor’s jerkyless feel. The scroll- *offset*is decoupled from row height (renderers paint at a- **fractional**pixel offset + clip), and the whole thing is- **deterministic under an injected clock**(- `advance(dt)`), so snapshots reproduce exactly (FC-7 / P0-5). Reusable by text, console, and the dataframe grid (SCRL-3).
- [theme](https://docs.rs/theme/index.html)
- **Theming.**A palette the custom-painted components (graph/depgraph/map) read from the egui context, plus matching egui- `Visuals`for the standard widgets (pop/table/pipeline). Call- `set_theme`- `Theme::default`- `Theme::sci_fi`- `Theme::nordic_aurora`- `Theme::cyberpunk_neon`- `Theme::amber_crt`- `Theme::deep_space`- `Theme::hugin_noir`- `Theme::ALL`- `Theme::by_name`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Arrow](https://docs.rs/struct.ArrowColumnRef.html)- Column - Ref
- One named Arrow column, shared zero-copy. The `Arc<dyn Array>`is the same buffer the source holds — copying a grid column never clones the data.
- [Edge](https://docs.rs/struct.Edge.html)
- A directed edge between node indices.
- [Facet](https://docs.rs/struct.FacetDeck.html)- Deck
- A tabbed set of `Facet`**every**facet’s`state_json`under its title, so the whole-app introspection contract is free. korp/nornir can build their window from a`FacetDeck`instead of hand-rolling tabs + the state dump.
- [KeyMap](https://docs.rs/struct.KeyMap.html)
- `Action → KeyboardShortcut`. Serialisable (KeyboardShortcut is serde in egui), so a host can save/load a remapped keymap (KEY-6). Uses- `Modifiers::COMMAND`which egui maps to ⌘ on macOS / Ctrl elsewhere (KEY-3).
- [Look](https://docs.rs/struct.LookTheme.html)- Theme
- The one theme (ARCH-1). Every sub-struct is fully populated by every preset
(no leaked defaults, ARCH-3); fields are public with `with_*`builders (ARCH-5); the whole thing is`serde`(ARCH-4).
- [Navigable](https://docs.rs/struct.Navigable.html)
- The shared pan/zoom model (NAV-1). Stores a scale + translation as a
`TSTransform`mapping**scene → screen**. Map, graph and plot all drive this with the same gestures, so they feel identical (NAV-2).
- [Node](https://docs.rs/struct.Node.html)
- A node: a label + a colour (the *consumer*picks the colour policy — hash by label, by status, …).
- [Scene](https://docs.rs/struct.Scene.html)
- A drawable graph: nodes + edges (edges index into `nodes`).
- [Smooth](https://docs.rs/struct.SmoothScroll.html)- Scroll
- A 1-D smooth scroll axis. `offset`is the current (fractional) pixel offset;`target`is where we’re easing toward;`velocity`carries momentum after a flick. Advance with`advance`
- [Theme](https://docs.rs/struct.Theme.html)
- The facett palette. All custom-painted colours come from here.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Action](https://docs.rs/enum.Action.html)
- The single semantic action vocabulary shared by every facett component
(COH-2). A given action is the **same chord in every component**because the chord lives only here, in the`KeyMap`
- [Clip](https://docs.rs/enum.ClipKind.html)- Kind
- The kinds a payload can take. `Custom`is the extension point.
- [Clip](https://docs.rs/enum.ClipPayload.html)- Payload
- A typed clipboard payload. The richest form a source can offer; a target picks
the best representation it accepts (negotiation in [`PasteTarget::paste`]).
- [Dir4](https://docs.rs/enum.Dir4.html)
- A compass direction for directional focus / pane moves.
- [Layout](https://docs.rs/enum.Layout.html)
- Node placement strategy.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Copy](https://docs.rs/trait.CopySource.html)- Source
- A component that can **produce**a typed payload from its current selection.
- [Facet](https://docs.rs/trait.Facet.html)
- The facett **component contract**. Every facet — graph, map, pipeline, table, the ported nornir viewers — implements this, so consumers (korp, nornir, …) compose them uniformly*and*get headless robot-testing for free.
- [Paste](https://docs.rs/trait.PasteTarget.html)- Target
- A component that can **accept**a pasted payload.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [draw](https://docs.rs/fn.draw.html)
- Draw a `Scene`into`ui`— the reusable render primitive. Empty scenes show`empty_hint`. Labels render when the node count is small enough to read.
- [hash_](https://docs.rs/fn.hash_color.html)- color
- A stable, bright-ish colour from a string (FNV-1a). Handy default node colour.
- [set_](https://docs.rs/fn.set_theme.html)- theme
- Store `theme`on the context**and**apply its egui`Visuals`. Call once per frame (cheap) or whenever the theme changes; every facet picks it up.
- [theme](https://docs.rs/fn.theme.html)
- The theme stored on the ui’s context (or `Theme::default`

# facett_map3d_flight - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-map3d-flight/0.1.10/facett_map3d_flight/

## Expand description

**facett-map3d-flight** — the AAA planetary **FLIGHT-SIM** engine layer over the
lightweight, embeddable [ facett_map3d](https://docs.rs/facett-map3d/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_map3d/index.html) map. This crate carries the heavy,
GPU-required, full-screen “bells and whistles”;

`facett-map3d` stays lean
(flat ground + extruded house markers, CPU-fallback, deck-pane-embeddable).[§](https://docs.rs#what-has-landed-here-cpu-foundation--build--test-green-headless)What has LANDED here (CPU foundation — build + test green, headless)

- `origin`- **floating origin**: an- `f64`Web-Mercator world frame + per-frame camera-centred rebase to- `f32`, killing far-from-origin vertex jitter / Z-fighting at planetary scale (FLIGHT-SIM #1).
- `atmos`- **precomputed atmospheric scattering**: a Bruneton/Hillaire-style transmittance LUT + single-scatter sky-view + aerial perspective, feeding both the sky AND the terrain/building haze, varying with altitude + sun angle (FLIGHT-SIM #2). Derived sky tints are ready to drive- `facett_map3d`’s existing analytic- `sky.wgsl`uniforms.
- `camera_fly`- **camera rig**: a deterministic 6DOF state machine (free-fly primary / cinematic orbit / flight-stick) over the- `f64`world frame, exercising the floating origin.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-is-roadmapped--spiked-see-nornirflightsim-engine-roadmapmd)What is ROADMAPPED / spiked (see `.nornir/flightsim-engine-roadmap.md`)

GPU scattering-LUT precompute pass, GPU-compute building extrusion (BuildingMeta
marshaller + indirect draw), CDLOD/quadtree DEM terrain + the drape fix, and the
out-of-core Hilbert-sorted GeoParquet streaming. The shared `Mesh3` + wgpu
pipeline + sky/water shaders are **reused** from `facett_map3d` (re-exported
below), not forked.

Everything that lands here is pure CPU math (no GPU, no egui at the foundation layer), so the precision + scattering + rig invariants are directly inject-assert-testable and deterministic (FC-7).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use atmos::`- [Atmosphere](https://docs.rs/atmos/struct.Atmosphere.html);
- `pub use atmos::`- [TransmittanceLut](https://docs.rs/atmos/struct.TransmittanceLut.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [atmos](https://docs.rs/atmos/index.html)
- **Precomputed atmospheric scattering**(FLIGHT-SIM #2) — a Bruneton/Hillaire- style physical sky that replaces the harsh distance-fog clip with real- **aerial perspective**, and makes the horizon curve, air density, and light colour change with- **altitude**and- **sun angle**.
- [camera_](https://docs.rs/camera_fly/index.html)- fly
- **Flight camera rig**(FLIGHT-SIM camera) — a deterministic, scriptable camera state machine over the- `f64`world frame, the rig that honestly exercises the- `crate::origin`
- [control](https://docs.rs/control/index.html)
- **egui →**— the “actually fly it” layer. A- `FlyInput`- `FlightController`- `camera_fly::FlyInput`] and drives a- `FlightCamera`
- [origin](https://docs.rs/origin/index.html)
- **Floating origin**— the foundational fix for- *far-from-origin vertex jitter*at planetary scale (FLIGHT-SIM #1).
- [sweden](https://docs.rs/sweden/index.html)
- **Sweden extent + a Web-Mercator slippy tile grid**— the spatial index that turns “fly the whole of Sweden” into a bounded, prioritisable set of tiles.
- [tiles](https://docs.rs/tiles/index.html)
- **Out-of-core tile streaming (§5)**— a background worker + an- `mpsc`- `Msg::TileLoaded`- `crate::sweden`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Mesh3](https://docs.rs/struct.Mesh3.html)
- Re-export the shared, reused pieces from the lightweight map so flight-sim
callers extend (not fork) them: the extruded mesh contract + the sun/sky model
(the seam the scattering plugs into) + the LOD ladder.
A 3D mesh of the extruded map: positions + per-vertex normals (parallel) +
per-**triangle**source colours + triangle indices. Coordinates are in the normalised`[-1, 1]`design box (x right,**y up**, z depth) with the ground at`y = 0`and prisms rising to`+height`.
- [SunSky](https://docs.rs/struct.SunSky.html)
- Re-export the shared, reused pieces from the lightweight map so flight-sim
callers extend (not fork) them: the extruded mesh contract + the sun/sky model
(the seam the scattering plugs into) + the LOD ladder.
A directional sun + sky environment. All colours are linear-ish `[r,g,b]`in`0..1`;`dir`points FROM the surface TO the sun (the convention the PBR shader’s`dot(n, l)`wants).

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [LodTier](https://docs.rs/enum.LodTier.html)
- Re-export the shared, reused pieces from the lightweight map so flight-sim
callers extend (not fork) them: the extruded mesh contract + the sun/sky model
(the seam the scattering plugs into) + the LOD ladder.
A camera-altitude detail tier. Gates which passes run + uniform flags +
resource sizes. The `< 300 m → reflective water`rule is the`Ground`tier.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [atmospheric_](https://docs.rs/fn.atmospheric_sunsky.html)- sunsky
- Bridge the `atmos::Atmosphere``facett_map3d`’s`SunSky``SunSky`whose`sky_color`is the atmosphere-derived**zenith**tint at the given altitude + sun, so the existing analytic GPU sky pass (and the CPU painter fog) become altitude/sun-driven with no new GPU pass. The horizon tint is returned alongside for the`sky.wgsl``horizon`uniform / the fog base colour.

# xcelerator_solver - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/xcelerator-solver/0.1.0/xcelerator_solver/

## Expand description

Xcelerator Solver — deterministic, precision-configurable symbolic regression engine.

Given tabular data (CSV) and an explicit vocabulary of allowed terms and operators, the solver exhaustively searches for mathematical expressions that explain the data within a user-specified error threshold.

[§](https://docs.rs#design-principles)Design principles

- **Deterministic**— Bottom-Up Enumeration (BUE) always finds the simplest formula at any error level first. Identical inputs produce identical results.
- **Explicit pool**— only declared terms and operators are used; no hidden defaults, no open-ended constant optimization.
- **Configurable precision**— expressions can be evaluated at arbitrary MPFR precision (- `--features hp`); named constants (- `Pi`,- `e`,- `gamma`, …) are materialized at full target precision via MPFR built-ins.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start-library-usage)Quick start (library usage)

```
use xcelerator_solver::{SolverConfig, solve};
let config = SolverConfig::load("solver.toml".as_ref()).unwrap();
let result = solve(config).unwrap();
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use config::`- [SolverConfig](https://docs.rs/config/struct.SolverConfig.html);
- `pub use output::`- [FinalEntry](https://docs.rs/output/struct.FinalEntry.html);
- `pub use output::`- [run_validation](https://docs.rs/output/fn.run_validation.html);
- `pub use output::`- [print_table](https://docs.rs/output/fn.print_table.html);
- `pub use output::`- [print_json](https://docs.rs/output/fn.print_json.html);
- `pub use output::`- [Tee](https://docs.rs/output/struct.Tee.html);
- `pub use pipeline::`- [PipelineResult](https://docs.rs/pipeline/struct.PipelineResult.html);
- `pub use pipeline::`- [SearchStats](https://docs.rs/pipeline/struct.SearchStats.html);
- `pub use pipeline::`- [run_pipeline](https://docs.rs/pipeline/fn.run_pipeline.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [aggregator](https://docs.rs/aggregator/index.html)
- Aggregator: bounded top-X heap, error-threshold filter, pinned check.
- [config](https://docs.rs/config/index.html)
- TOML configuration loading and validation for the solver.
- [csv_](https://docs.rs/csv_loader/index.html)- loader
- CSV parsing into DataPoints (f64 and HP variants).
- [error_](https://docs.rs/error_metric/index.html)- metric
- MAPE, MAE, and RMSE error metrics — f64 and HP variants.
- [eval](https://docs.rs/eval/index.html)
- f64 expression evaluator.
- [evaluator](https://docs.rs/evaluator/index.html)
- Evaluator worker pool.
- [expr](https://docs.rs/expr/index.html)
- Expression AST: types, canonical form, display, subtree containment.
- [generator](https://docs.rs/generator/index.html)
- Streaming candidate generator — two-level parallel design.
- [output](https://docs.rs/output/index.html)
- Output module: validation scoring, table/JSON formatting, Tee writer.
- [pinned](https://docs.rs/pinned/index.html)
- Pinned sub-components: expression string parser and containment check.
- [pipeline](https://docs.rs/pipeline/index.html)
- Pipeline wiring: owns VisitedSet, spawns threads, connects all actors.
- [vocabulary](https://docs.rs/vocabulary/index.html)
- Vocabulary: allowed terms, operators, constants, and seed expressions. Maps spelled-out config names (“add”, “multiply”, “Pi”) to typed values.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [solve](https://docs.rs/fn.solve.html)
- Run the solver end-to-end.

# mongreldb_kit - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mongreldb-kit/0.9.0/mongreldb_kit/

## Expand description

Storage-backed MongrelDB Kit crate.

This crate wraps MongrelDB core with the kit schema model, transaction semantics, query execution, and migration runner.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use db::`- [ApproxAggKind](https://docs.rs/db/enum.ApproxAggKind.html);
- `pub use db::`- [ApproxAggregate](https://docs.rs/db/struct.ApproxAggregate.html);
- `pub use db::`- [Database](https://docs.rs/db/struct.Database.html);
- `pub use db::`- [ExplainPlan](https://docs.rs/db/struct.ExplainPlan.html);
- `pub use db::`- [IncrementalAggKind](https://docs.rs/db/enum.IncrementalAggKind.html);
- `pub use db::`- [IncrementalAggregate](https://docs.rs/db/struct.IncrementalAggregate.html);
- `pub use db::`- [SimilarRow](https://docs.rs/db/struct.SimilarRow.html);
- `pub use error::`- [KitError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.KitError.html);
- `pub use error::`- [Result](https://docs.rs/error/type.Result.html);
- `pub use migrate::`- [migrate](https://docs.rs/migrate/fn.migrate.html);
- `pub use query::`- [JoinRow](https://docs.rs/query/type.JoinRow.html);
- `pub use schema::`- [Row](https://docs.rs/schema/struct.Row.html);
- `pub use txn::`- [Transaction](https://docs.rs/txn/struct.Transaction.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [check](https://docs.rs/check/index.html)
- Evaluation of table/column check constraints.
- [db](https://docs.rs/db/index.html)
- Database handle for `mongreldb-kit`.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Error model for `mongreldb-kit`.
- [keys](https://docs.rs/keys/index.html)
- Key encoding for Kit indexes, guards, and primary keys.
- [migrate](https://docs.rs/migrate/index.html)
- Migration runner for `mongreldb-kit`.
- [migrations](https://docs.rs/migrations/index.html)
- Migration planning and checksums.
- [planner](https://docs.rs/planner/index.html)
- Delete planning: compute the set of rows affected by a delete, including cascade, set-null, and restrict foreign-key actions.
- [procedure](https://docs.rs/procedure/index.html)
- [pushdown](https://docs.rs/pushdown/index.html)
- Predicate pushdown: translate Kit `Expr`predicates into MongrelDB core`Condition`s so the native engine can resolve them via indexes instead of a full-scan + Rust evaluation (Kit Priority 1).
- [query](https://docs.rs/query/index.html)
- Query execution for kit statements.
- [schema](https://docs.rs/schema/index.html)
- Schema/value conversion between the kit model and MongrelDB core.
- [tsv](https://docs.rs/tsv/index.html)
- TSV import/export for kit tables.
- [txn](https://docs.rs/txn/index.html)
- Kit transaction wrapper around a MongrelDB core transaction.
- [validation](https://docs.rs/validation/index.html)
- Row validation against a `Table`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Aggregate](https://docs.rs/struct.Aggregate.html)
- A single aggregate output column, e.g. `SUM(total) AS total_sum`.
- [Aggregate](https://docs.rs/struct.AggregateQuery.html)- Query
- A grouped/aggregated query. Rows are scanned, optionally filtered, grouped by
`group_by`key columns, reduced with`aggregates`, and finally filtered by`having`. With no`group_by`, the whole (filtered) table is one group.
- [Check](https://docs.rs/struct.CheckConstraint.html)- Constraint
- A named table-level check constraint.
- [Check](https://docs.rs/struct.CheckParseError.html)- Parse - Error
- Error produced when a check expression cannot be parsed.
- [Column](https://docs.rs/struct.Column.html)
- A column definition.
- [Cte](https://docs.rs/struct.Cte.html)
- A common table expression: a named, materialized subquery. A later query can
read from `name`as if it were a table.
- [Delete](https://docs.rs/struct.Delete.html)
- A `DELETE`statement.
- [Delete](https://docs.rs/struct.DeletePlan.html)- Plan
- Result of planning a delete against a schema.
- [Foreign](https://docs.rs/struct.ForeignKey.html)- Key
- A foreign-key reference from child columns to parent columns.
- [Index](https://docs.rs/struct.Index.html)
- An index on one or more columns.
- [Insert](https://docs.rs/struct.Insert.html)
- An `INSERT`statement.
- [Join](https://docs.rs/struct.Join.html)
- One joined table in a `JoinQuery`
- [Join](https://docs.rs/struct.JoinQuery.html)- Query
- A nested-loop join query. The result is a list of combined rows; each combined
row is a JSON object keyed by table alias whose values are that source’s row
object (or JSON `null`for an unmatched right side of a`LEFT`join). Column references in`filter`/`order_by`/join`on`must be qualified (`alias.column`).
- [Migration](https://docs.rs/struct.Migration.html)
- A numbered schema migration.
- [OrderBy](https://docs.rs/struct.OrderBy.html)
- An `ORDER BY`clause.
- [Procedure](https://docs.rs/struct.ProcedureSpec.html)- Spec
- [Restricted](https://docs.rs/struct.RestrictedConstraint.html)- Constraint
- A foreign-key constraint that blocks the delete.
- [RowRef](https://docs.rs/struct.RowRef.html)
- A row identified for deletion planning.
- [Schema](https://docs.rs/struct.Schema.html)
- A validated collection of tables.
- [Select](https://docs.rs/struct.Select.html)
- A `SELECT`statement.
- [Sequence](https://docs.rs/struct.Sequence.html)
- A monotonic sequence allocator.
- [SetNull](https://docs.rs/struct.SetNullUpdate.html)- Update
- A child row that must be updated to set its foreign-key columns to null.
- [Table](https://docs.rs/struct.Table.html)
- A table definition.
- [Unique](https://docs.rs/struct.UniqueConstraint.html)- Constraint
- A uniqueness constraint over one or more columns.
- [Update](https://docs.rs/struct.Update.html)
- An `UPDATE`statement.
- [Upsert](https://docs.rs/struct.Upsert.html)
- An `UPSERT`statement.
- [Validation](https://docs.rs/struct.ValidationError.html)- Error
- A validation failure returned by `validate_row`

# ggen_a2a_mcp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ggen-a2a-mcp/26.7.2/ggen_a2a_mcp/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#ggen-a2a-mcp---agent-to-agent-protocol-and-mcp-server)ggen-a2a-mcp - Agent-to-Agent Protocol and MCP Server

A2A protocol implementation for agent-to-agent communication with Model Context Protocol (MCP) server support.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- Task state machine protocol
- Artifact and artifact collection types
- In-process and external transport support
- Multi-agent orchestration registry
- Health monitoring and status tracking

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [a2a](https://docs.rs/a2a/index.html)
- Agent-to-Agent Task State Machine Protocol

- A2A-RS Integration Code
- [a2a_](https://docs.rs/a2a_registry/index.html)- registry
- `ggen-a2a-registry`– Multi-agent A2A orchestration registry.
- [mcp_](https://docs.rs/mcp_packs/index.html)- packs
- Pack + marketplace tools for the agent surface (MCP and A2A).
- [mcp_](https://docs.rs/mcp_server/index.html)- server

# mongreldb_kit_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mongreldb-kit-core/0.9.0/mongreldb_kit_core/

## Expand description

Core, language-neutral model for MongrelDB Kit.

This crate contains the schema model, key encoding, validation, constraint
planning, migration planning, and query AST used by the storage-backed
`mongreldb-kit` crate and by language bindings.

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap

## Expand description

Command Line Argument Parser for Rust

Quick Links:

- Derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
- Builder [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- [Cookbook](https://docs.rs/_cookbook/index.html)
- [CLI Concepts](https://docs.rs/_concepts/index.html)
- [FAQ](https://docs.rs/_faq/index.html)
- [Discussions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/discussions)
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v4.6.1/CHANGELOG.md)(includes major version migration guides)

[§](https://docs.rs#aspirations)Aspirations

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

- We follow semver and will wait about 6-9 months between major breaking changes
- We will support the last two minor Rust releases (MSRV, currently 1.74)

While these aspirations can be at odds with fast build times and low binary
size, we will still strive to keep these reasonable for the flexibility you
get.  Check out the
[argparse-benchmarks](https://github.com/rust-cli/argparse-benchmarks-rs) for
CLI parsers optimized for other use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Run

`$ cargo add clap --features derive`*(See also  feature flag reference)*

Then define your CLI in `main.rs`:

```
use clap::Parser;
/// Simple program to greet a person
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)]
struct Args {
    /// Name of the person to greet
    #[arg(short, long)]
    name: String,
    /// Number of times to greet
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)]
    count: u8,
}
fn main() {
    let args = Args::parse();
    for _ in 0..args.count {
        println!("Hello {}!", args.name);
    }
}
```
And try it out:

```
$ demo --help
A simple to use, efficient, and full-featured Command Line Argument Parser
Usage: demo[EXE] [OPTIONS] --name <NAME>
Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

See also the derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html) and [reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)

[§](https://docs.rs#related-projects)Related Projects

Augment clap:

- [wild](https://crates.io/crates/wild)for supporting wildcards (- `*`) on Windows like you do Linux
- [argfile](https://crates.io/crates/argfile)for loading additional arguments from a file (aka response files)
- [shadow-rs](https://crates.io/crates/shadow-rs)for generating- `Command::long_version`
- [clap_mangen](https://crates.io/crates/clap_mangen)for generating man page source (roff)
- [clap_complete](https://crates.io/crates/clap_complete)for shell completion support
- [clap-i18n-richformatter](https://crates.io/crates/clap-i18n-richformatter)for i18n support with- `clap::error::RichFormatter`

CLI Helpers

- [clio](https://crates.io/crates/clio)for reading/writing to files specified as arguments
- [clap-verbosity-flag](https://crates.io/crates/clap-verbosity-flag)
- [clap-cargo](https://crates.io/crates/clap-cargo)
- [colorchoice-clap](https://crates.io/crates/colorchoice-clap)

Testing

- `trycmd`
- `snapbox`
- `assert_cmd`- `assert_fs`

Documentation:

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- CLI Concepts

- Documentation: Cookbook

- Error reporting

- `Command`

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [arg](https://docs.rs/macro.arg.html)
- Create an `Arg`
- [command](https://docs.rs/macro.command.html)- `cargo`
- Allows you to build the `Command`instance from your Cargo.toml at compile time.
- [crate_](https://docs.rs/macro.crate_authors.html)- authors - `cargo`
- Allows you to pull the authors for the command from your Cargo.toml at
compile time in the form:
`"author1 lastname <author1@example.com>:author2 lastname <author2@example.com>"`
- [crate_](https://docs.rs/macro.crate_description.html)- description - `cargo`
- Allows you to pull the description from your Cargo.toml at compile time.
- [crate_](https://docs.rs/macro.crate_name.html)- name - `cargo`
- Allows you to pull the name from your Cargo.toml at compile time.
- [crate_](https://docs.rs/macro.crate_version.html)- version - `cargo`
- Allows you to pull the version from your Cargo.toml at compile time as
`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH_PKGVERSION_PRE`
- [value_](https://docs.rs/macro.value_parser.html)- parser
- Select a `ValueParser`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Arg](https://docs.rs/struct.Arg.html)
- The abstract representation of a command line argument. Used to set all the options and relationships that define a valid argument for the program.
- [ArgGroup](https://docs.rs/struct.ArgGroup.html)
- Specifies a logical group of [arguments](https://docs.rs/struct.Arg.html)
- [ArgMatches](https://docs.rs/struct.ArgMatches.html)
- Container for parse results.
- [Command](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- Build a command-line interface.
- [Id](https://docs.rs/struct.Id.html)
- `Arg`- `ArgGroup`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [ArgAction](https://docs.rs/enum.ArgAction.html)
- Behavior of arguments when they are encountered while parsing
- [Color](https://docs.rs/enum.ColorChoice.html)- Choice
- Represents the color preferences for program output
- [Value](https://docs.rs/enum.ValueHint.html)- Hint
- Provide shell with hint on how to complete an argument.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Args](https://docs.rs/trait.Args.html)
- Parse a set of arguments into a user-defined container.
- [Command](https://docs.rs/trait.CommandFactory.html)- Factory
- Create a `Command`
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromArgMatches.html)- ArgMatches
- Converts an instance of `ArgMatches`
- [Parser](https://docs.rs/trait.Parser.html)
- Parse command-line arguments into `Self`.
- [Subcommand](https://docs.rs/trait.Subcommand.html)
- Parse a sub-command into a user-defined enum.
- [Value](https://docs.rs/trait.ValueEnum.html)- Enum
- Parse arguments into enums.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/type.Error.html)
- Command Line Argument Parser Error
